HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P)

History:
• Presenting complaint: 2-3 day history of increased shortness of breath, wheeze, and dry cough.  
• Onset/Progression: Noticed while running with friend; now occurs with brisk walking. Symptoms persistent despite salbutamol.  
• Associated symptoms: Wheeze; denies sputum production; no mention of chest pain or fever.  
• Triggers: Physical exertion.  
• Previous asthma control: Last exacerbation 3-4 years ago; no prior hospital admissions, oral steroids, or antibiotics.  
• Home peak-flow baseline ≈ 380 L/min; no recent measurement.  

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (childhood-onset, previously well-controlled).  
• Hay fever.  
• Possible eczema (self-reported; family history positive).  
• No past hospitalizations for asthma; last asthma review ≈ 2 years ago.  

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler (blue) – dose/route/frequency: PRN, “every 2–4 h” currently.  
• Clenil (brown inhaler) – currently 3 puffs twice daily; plan to increase (see Plan).  
• “Flanel Bactroban” – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Cetraben – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Hydrocortisone (topical) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Physical Examination:
(teleconsultation – no direct exam)  
• Subjective wheeze reported.  
• No sputum production.  
• No prior hospital admissions; alert and interactive on video.  

Impression:
• Likely mild asthma exacerbation.

Management Plan:
• Increase Clenil to 4 puffs twice daily until reviewed.  
• Continue salbutamol inhaler up to every 2 h PRN.  
• Arrange face-to-face GP review within a few days for chest exam, peak-flow measurement, and assessment for possible oral steroids or antibiotics.  
• Emergency advice: Attend A&E if breathing deteriorates, salbutamol required very frequently, or unable to wait for GP review.  

Patient Summary:
Adult with long-standing asthma reports new 2-3 day episode of exertional dyspnoea and wheeze unrelieved by usual salbutamol. No sputum, fever, or previous severe attacks. Plan is to step-up inhaled steroid, monitor, and obtain urgent in-person assessment.

Key Takeaways:
• Increase brown inhaler (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily.  
• Use blue inhaler only as needed, up to every 2 h; if this becomes necessary frequently, seek urgent care.  
• Book face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for full asthma review.

Next Steps:
• Record peak-flow readings at home and bring to appointment.  
• GP to consider oral steroids/antibiotics based on examination findings.  
• Schedule routine annual asthma review once acute episode resolves.
